## What this file is

This file walks you through turning your White Paper project into the two things you submit:
a PDF and a live website. You will give your Results chapter its data, write a sentence whose
numbers come from the code, add a figure that redraws itself, render the whole paper, and
publish it.

Every gray box below is a **code chunk**. Click **Run Cell** at its top left corner, or click
inside the box and press **Ctrl+Enter** (Windows) or **Cmd+Enter** (Mac). Under each box this
file tells you what should appear and what to do when it does not.

Some boxes are not for running here. Those are marked **Paste this into
`03-results.qmd`**: they are written for your Results chapter, and they only work there.

Save this file in the **top folder** of your workspace, next to `README.md`, and open it from
there. The guide *Put a Worksheet in Your Workspace* shows how, step by step:
[MC 451](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/guides/mc451/14-put-a-worksheet-in-your-workspace.html)
or [MC 501](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/guides/mc501/14-put-a-worksheet-in-your-workspace.html).
Your White Paper project is the folder you made with the Chapter 9 file
(`09-coding-the-codebook.qmd`).

The examples below use the Twitch data from the three worksheets, so you can see each step
work before you change it. Your paper reports your own study: wherever a box names
`twitch_analysis.RDS`, `message_length`, or `channel_type`, use your own file and your own
variables.

## Step 1: Switch the course package on and check its version

Publishing needs version 0.3.6 of the course package or newer. Earlier versions stop at the
last step with `Publish failed:` and nothing after it.

```{r}
library(v2v)
packageVersion("v2v")
```

**What you should see:** a short startup message, then `[1] '0.3.6'` or a higher number.

**If the number is lower than 0.3.6,** close VS Code, open plain R (the R program itself, not
VS Code), and run the line below. Answer no to any question about updating other packages,
then open VS Code again and rerun this step.

```{r}
remotes::install_github("AURA-Lab-SIUE/v2v-r", upgrade = "never")
```

## Step 2: Point R at your White Paper project

This names your project folder once, so every later step can use it. **Change the name inside
the quotes to the name you used in the Chapter 9 file.** If you do not remember it, it is the
folder holding `_quarto.yml` and `01-introduction.qmd` in the **Explorer** panel.

```{r}
project <- "twitch-portfolio"                      # your project folder's name
file.exists(file.path(project, "_quarto.yml"))     # TRUE means R found it
```

**What you should see:** `[1] TRUE`.

**If you see `[1] FALSE`,** the name in the quotes does not match your folder. Check the
spelling against the Explorer panel, including capital letters and hyphens, and run the step
again.

## Step 3: Install the PDF tool

Your paper renders to a website and a PDF. The website needs nothing new. The PDF needs a
typesetting program called **TinyTeX**, which most computers do not have. Without it, the
render stops with `No TeX installation was detected`.

This step is not R code. Open the **Terminal** panel in VS Code (**Terminal**, then **New
Terminal**), type this line, and press Enter:

```bash
quarto install tinytex
```

It downloads for a few minutes. When it finishes, quit VS Code completely and open it again,
then run this line in the same Terminal:

```bash
quarto check
```

**What you should see:** under **Checking LaTeX**, a `Version:` line with a year.

**If it says `Tex: (not detected)`,** the install did not finish. Run `quarto install tinytex`
again and read the last lines it prints; if they show an error, email me that text.

Then come back to this file and run Step 1 and Step 2 again, since quitting VS Code ended the R
session. Last, check for the small R package that hands your project to Quarto:

```{r}
if (!requireNamespace("quarto", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("quarto")                       # only if it is missing
}
```

**What you should see:** nothing if you already had it, or an install that ends with a line
about the downloaded packages.

## Step 4: Put your analysis file inside the project

Your Results chapter renders from inside the project folder, so the file it reads has to be
inside that folder too. The Data Wrangling worksheet saved `twitch_analysis.RDS` in the `data`
folder at the top of your workspace. This copies it into the project's `data/derived` folder.

```{r}
file.copy(
  from = "data/twitch_analysis.RDS",                         # where the worksheet saved it
  to   = file.path(project, "data", "derived"),              # where the paper reads it
  overwrite = TRUE                                           # replace an older copy
)

list.files(file.path(project, "data", "derived"))            # what is there now
```

**What you should see:** `[1] TRUE`, then `[1] "twitch_analysis.RDS"`.

**If you see `[1] FALSE` and a warning that begins `problem copying`,** R could not find the file to copy. Check that `twitch_analysis.RDS`
is in the `data` folder next to your worksheets, or change the `from` line to where it is.

## Step 5: Load the data the way your Results chapter will

Before you write anything in the paper, check that the copy loads and has the rows you expect.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

analysis <- read_rds(file.path(project, "data", "derived", "twitch_analysis.RDS"))
nrow(analysis)                                   # one row per message
```

**What you should see:** the list of attached packages, then `[1] 35267`.

**If you see `cannot open the connection`,** Step 4 did not copy the file. Run Step 4 again.

## Step 6: Give your Results chapter its own setup chunk

Each chapter of the paper starts from nothing when it renders, so `03-results.qmd` needs its
own lines that switch the packages on and load the data. `include: false` runs the chunk
but leaves both the code and its output out of the paper.

**Paste this into `03-results.qmd`,** on a new line under the guidance text, then save the
file:

````markdown
```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(v2v)
analysis <- read_rds("data/derived/twitch_analysis.RDS")
```
````

The path here is shorter than the one in Step 5, because the chapter runs from inside the
project folder, where `data` sits at the top.

## Step 7: Write a sentence whose numbers come from the code

A number you type by hand goes stale the moment your data changes. A number written as inline
code is computed again on every render. `format(..., big.mark = ",")` prints `35267` as
`35,267`, the way a reader expects to see it.

**Paste this into `03-results.qmd`,** under the setup chunk, then save the file:

```markdown
The analysis dataset held `r format(nrow(analysis), big.mark = ",")` messages,
of which `r format(nrow(drop_na(analysis, channel_type)), big.mark = ",")`
carried a channel type.
```

You will see the result in Step 9. In the rendered paper it reads: *The analysis dataset held
35,267 messages, of which 34,766 carried a channel type.*

Now find one number in your own Results that you typed by hand, and replace it the same way.

## Step 8: Add a figure that redraws itself

A figure made by a chunk in the paper is drawn again on every render, so it always matches the
data. The `label` must start with `fig-`; that is what lets you refer to the figure by number.
`echo: false` shows the figure without the code that made it.

**Paste this into `03-results.qmd`,** under the sentence from Step 7, then save the file:

````markdown
```{r}
#| label: fig-length
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Message length by channel type."
analysis %>%
  filter(!is.na(channel_type), message_length <= 200) %>%   # the longest messages left off the axis
  ggplot(aes(x = message_length, fill = channel_type)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
  scale_fill_v2v() +
  labs(x = "Characters per message", y = "Messages", fill = "Channel type") +
  theme_v2v()
```

@fig-length shows how long messages run in each kind of channel.
````

The last line refers to the figure by its label. In the rendered paper `@fig-length` becomes a
link with the figure's number in it, and Quarto keeps the numbers right as you add figures.

## Step 9: Preview the Results chapter

With `03-results.qmd` open, click the **Preview** button at the top right of the editor, or
press **Ctrl+Shift+K** (Windows) or **Cmd+Shift+K** (Mac).

**What you should see:** after a few seconds, a preview pane with the guidance text, your
sentence with the real counts in it, and the histogram with its caption underneath.

**If you see `object 'analysis' not found`,** the setup chunk from Step 6 is missing or sits
below the sentence. It has to come first.

**If you see `cannot open the connection`,** the data file is not inside the project. Run Step 4
again.

## Step 10: Render the whole paper

Preview shows one chapter. Rendering builds every chapter into the website and the PDF in one
pass. Close the preview pane first.

```{r}
quarto::quarto_render(project)
```

**What you should see:** a stream of lines about each chapter, a section headed `Rendering
PDF`, and last `Output created: docs/index.html`. A `docs` folder appears inside your project,
and inside it a PDF named after your paper's title (`White-Paper.pdf` until you change the
title in `_quarto.yml`).

**If you see `No TeX installation was detected`,** TinyTeX is missing. Go back to Step 3.

**If it stops at one chapter with an error,** the error names the chapter and the line. Fix
that line, save, and run this step again.

## Step 11: Read the PDF

The PDF is what you upload, so read it the way a grader will. This opens it in your PDF reader.

```{r}
browseURL(file.path(project, "docs", "White-Paper.pdf"))
```

**What you should see:** a title page and a table of contents, then the abstract, every section
in order, the references, and the codebook and journal as appendices.

**If you see an error that the file does not exist,** your title is no longer "White Paper," so
the PDF has another name. Open the `docs` folder in the Explorer panel to find it.

## Step 12: Commit and push

Publishing sends what you last committed, so commit first. In the **Source Control** panel,
write a message such as `Results chapter and first full render`, click **Commit**, then click
**Sync Changes**. `01-commit-your-work.qmd` walks through this panel step by step.

Your commit includes the project's `.gitignore`, which Quarto edits on the first render, and
the `docs` folder. Commit both.

**What you should see:** the Source Control panel empties, and the files appear on your
repository's page on GitHub.

## Step 13: Publish

This runs three checks, renders the paper again, and sends the site to GitHub Pages. Your
project already sits inside your workspace repository, which is already on GitHub, so the site
is published from that repository.

```{r}
v2v::deploy_portfolio(project)
```

Partway through it asks `Publish to GitHub Pages? [y/N]`. Click in the R console, type `y`, and
press Enter. If a GitHub sign-in window opens, sign in; it is the same sign-in as your first
push.

**What you should see:** under **Pre-flight checks**, green check marks beside `no uncommitted
changes` and `_quarto.yml valid` (the line saying no `renv.lock` was found is normal), a render,
then `Publishing to GitHub Pages` and last `Portfolio live on GitHub Pages.`

**If you see `uncommitted changes detected`,** the files listed under it are saved but not
committed. Do Step 12 again, then this step.

**If you see `Render failed`,** read the lines above it. `No TeX installation was detected`
means Step 3; anything else names the chapter and line to fix.

**If you see `not connected to a GitHub repository`,** your workspace was never pushed to
GitHub. Do `01-commit-your-work.qmd` first.

## Step 14: Open your site in a private window

Your address is `https://YOUR-GITHUB-USERNAME.github.io/YOUR-REPOSITORY-NAME/`, with your GitHub
username and the name of your workspace repository. GitHub takes a minute or two to put it up.

Open that address in a **private** or **incognito** window. That is how a reader without your
GitHub account sees it, and a paper nobody can open scores nothing.

**What you should see:** your paper as a website, one chapter per page, with the chapters listed
down the left side.

**If you still see a 404 page after five minutes,** stop and email me the full text Step 13
printed. Do not try to publish by hand through the GitHub settings pages.

## Every time you change the paper

Save, commit and push (Step 12), then publish again (Step 13). The site updates within a minute
or two. You do not need Steps 1 to 4 again unless you open a new R session; then run Step 1 and
Step 2 first.

## When a line breaks

R returns an error message instead of a result. The usual causes are a misspelling, a package
that is not switched on, or a path that points at the wrong folder. It happens to everyone and
it says nothing about your ability. Read the message before you retype anything; the wording is
the diagnosis.

For errors specific to the course package, run this in the R console:

```{r}
?v2v::common_errors
```

If you are still stuck after fifteen minutes, email me the **exact** text of the error, or a
screenshot, and the step number you were on.

## You are done when

- `03-results.qmd` reads its data in a setup chunk, and at least one sentence takes its numbers
  from inline code
- At least one figure in the paper is made by a chunk, not pasted in
- The `docs` folder holds a PDF with every section in it
- `v2v::deploy_portfolio()` ended with `Portfolio live on GitHub Pages.`, and your address opens
  in a private window

What you submit, and where, is on your course's assignments page under **White Paper**.
